data.title: Muromar the Dreadful – a pagan legend from the Papradno valley
data.excerpt: Another legend from pagan times recorded by Štefan Meliš and Stanislav Muntág, this time from the Papradno valley. A three-headed monster, Muromar, wakes in the bowels of the Žiar hill and lays waste the whole country, until the woodcutter Kondál goes against him with an axe enchanted by an old pagan priest.
data.metaTitle: Muromar the Dreadful – a legend from Papradno
data.metaDescription: A legend from pagan times from the Papradno valley: the three-headed monster Muromar wakes beneath the Žiar hill and the woodcutter Kondál fights him.

timeline.year: the arrival of the first Slavs
timeline.title: The country by the lake below Žiar is settled
timeline.description: The first Slavs came to the valley below Javorník, settled by the lake and, by burning off the crown of the hill (called Žiar ever since), woke the monster Muromar hidden in its bowels.

timeline.title: Muromar torments the country
timeline.description: The three-headed monster Muromar settled on the summit of Žiar, belched fire and brought disaster upon the country – the cattle gave no more milk and the crops withered.

timeline.title: Kondál kills Muromar
timeline.description: With an axe enchanted by the old pagan priest, the woodcutter Kondál defeated the three-headed Muromar, saved his bride Svatava and brought the priest the monster’s three heads.

children.text: And here we have yet another wonderful legend from pagan times by Mr Meliš and Mr Muntág, this time from the Papradno valley.

It was a terribly long time ago. The whole Papradno valley was covered with deep mountain forests, where centuries-old trees grew that not even two men could reach around with their arms. Firs and spruces, beeches, oaks, birches, maples and all manner of other trees. In the middle of the forests lay a great, deep lake. It stretched from Žeravica all the way to Košiare. The lake had no name, for in those days there was not a single person far and wide to give it one.

Then one day the first people came to this country – the Slavs. They had wandered in from somewhere on the Ukrainian steppes, pushed out by other, more warlike tribes, and in the mountains of present-day Slovakia they sought both shelter and a living. One family strayed into the deep valley below Javorník and came as far as the enchanted lake in the middle of the forests, above which a stern stone guardian rose into the sky – the hill known today as Žiar.

The ancient newcomers took a liking to this country and settled on the shore of the lake beneath the steep slopes of the hill. They felled and grubbed out the forest, ploughed the land and sowed grain. They burned off the crown of the hill – a tremendous flame blazed up and its glow (žiara) radiated far and wide. Ever since, this hill has been called Žiar. On the bared crown of the hill they meant to build a sacrificial site to their gods and a watchtower.

They did not know that the hill already had an inhabitant. Deep in the rocky cavities of the mountain, which reach down somewhere into the glowing underworld, there dwelt a hideous monster! He was not at all pleased that those earthly worms who had wandered in from somewhere were making a racket on the hill, burning trees and digging in the ground. Now and then the monster gave a sullen, warning roar. The hill shook and the people took fright, thinking that some volcano or earthquake was waking to life here; but when the mountain fell quiet again, they put the matter out of their heads and went back to their work.

In one little valley, cut deep into the stony body of Žiar, at the place today called Suchá, a young woodcutter settled at that time. Kondál was his name, and he was enormously strong, a fellow as big as a mountain. He made his living felling old trees, and he had plenty to do, for people needed good, thick beams to build cottages, pigsties and sheepfolds. Kondál prospered; he built up a farm, and a mistress for it was already in sight. For he had fallen in love with a beautiful maiden – Svatava was her name – and she was glad indeed to take such a handsome young man. They were preparing the wedding.

One day the earth shook again. The shepherds had just driven their herd of cows out onto Podžiarie and had grazed their way across the lush meadow as far as the locality known as Kopence, where a broad grassy saddle breaks the sharp ridge that runs like the back of a prehistoric lizard from the valley through Lazy right up to the very crown of the hill. All at once the cows began to bellow in panic. They left the pasture be, lifted their tails and ran up and down.

What has got into them today? the shepherds wonder. What the devil has frightened them? No storm is coming, the sky is clear, and there is not a bear or any other beast far and wide. In vain the shepherds rack their brains over the riddle. Something menacing hangs in the air. Suddenly the cows huddle close together, bellowing desperately and staring at one spot in the middle of the meadow. The shepherds’ dogs too tuck in their tails and whine in fear at their masters’ feet. Lads, these are no good omens! says the oldest shepherd. Something is happening!

Then the earth shook. The shepherds all but fell off their feet. At the very spot the cows had been gaping at in terror the meadow tore open, the air whistled and a whirlwind carried clumps of turf into the sky. A hideous three-headed monster clambered out of the hole and roared in anger, flames blazing from its nostrils, the air stinking of sulphur and ammonia. The monster looked around and lumbered clumsily up to the summit of Žiar. There it made itself at home. For many days the monster sat on the crown of Žiar. From time to time it roared in anger until the mountains shook, and belched flames from its nostrils. The people were terribly afraid of it. The cattle would not graze and only bellowed in panic in their byres. The hens stopped laying eggs, the cows lost their milk as well, the crops in the fields withered. Disaster came upon the whole country.
In vain the people called upon the old gods, brought offerings, prayed and begged Perún to strike the monster down with lightning. There was no help for them.

Only Kondál was not afraid. In the Mrská wood, which clothes the steep rocky flank of Žiar, he went on felling trees, sending them down the impassable precipice and preparing the timber for merchants in the valley, as though nothing out of the ordinary were happening.
„Kondál, Kondál“, the people shake their heads, „you will come to a bad end! Muromar himself will punish you.“
„Indeed“, others join in, „it was because of your racket that he woke and crawled out of the earth.“

„That is so“, still others agree, „it was in Mrská itself, where you cut your timber, that he had his lair. There among the rocks is the dragon’s hole, through which he looked out at the world, and you disturbed him.“

Kondál, however, paid no heed to such talk and went on cutting timber. He no longer even came down to the village, so that people should not pester him with their idle chatter. Now and then he would go to the lake on the valley floor to catch fish, and then straight home to Suchá, or else straight off to Mrská to cut wood.
„That Kondál of yours is to blame for everything“, the people say to Svatava, „he is felling in Mrská, by the dragon’s hole. And he will not be told. He has brought misfortune upon us.“

Svatava set off after Kondál with tears in her eyes. As she ran along the meadow path below Žiar, a dark cloud suddenly came down from the sky. Svatava never reached Kondál. People only came to tell him:
„Muromar has carried off your bride. Who knows whether the poor girl is still breathing.“

A terrible anger flared up in Kondál. He seized his sharp axe and set off into the mountains. But he did not go after Muromar; he went to that lonely hut below Javorník which everyone avoided from afar. For in it lived the old Žrec, a pagan priest who knew all manner of spells and was in league with every kind of unclean power. He had barely caught sight of Kondál when he smiled beneath his long moustache.
„Muromar is vexing you, is he?“ he asked the young man, though he knew the answer well and had long known everything.
Then he went on. „Muromar is a mighty demon, but I am mightier, by Perún!“

He took Kondál’s axe, thrust it into the embers, threw in some mysterious herbs and spoke magic incantations. The embers at once blazed up with an acrid flame, so that Kondál took fright that his axe would burn away entirely. But the old man drew it, red-hot as it was, out of the fire with his bare hand, and shortly afterwards handed it to Kondál.
„There, and now go and strike off Muromar’s heads. And bring them to me here. All three. I shall find a use for them!“ said the old Žrec.
Kondál runs, he clambers up to the summit of Žiar, looking out for the monster.

„Come out then, you hellish beast! Are you hiding from me, coward? Come out and let it be seen who is the stronger!“ he cried with all his might. There was a rumble and a flame flashed on the crown of the hill. Fearlessly Kondál climbs higher and higher. He is already on the last clearing below the sharp peak of Žiar. All at once the trees cracked. A sturdy spruce fell as if cut down, and a monstrous boulder came hurtling out of the forest straight at Kondál. He had no time to do anything but instinctively raise the hand holding the axe. The stone stopped before him halfway down the slope.
„Good spells that old wizard has!“ – the young man breathes out and, emboldened, quickens his step.

He is already within reach of the summit; already he smells the stench of sulphur and ammonia and hears the dull rasping of the monster and the faint moan of his beloved Svatava, who lies beside the beast, imprisoned by thorny scrub. Muromar roared again. It rose into the air and darkened the sun with its membranous wings. Three hideous heads stare fixedly at Kondál, spewing fire, sulphur and a frightful stench. A tremendous fight broke out. Kondál strikes with his axe into the monster’s body; Muromar writhes, roars, tries to burn the young man with its scorching breath, to cut him in two with its toothed tail, sharp as a razor, or to crush him under its monstrous paw. Kondál twists and turns like a madman. He fights, he wrestles with superhuman strength, but he is already weakening. His head is spinning, the beast’s poisonous breath has dazed him. The monster sees that Kondál is at his last gasp. Again it roars terribly, and the largest of its heads is already drawing near to burn the human worm to a cinder with a single breath.

Then Kondál swung his arm and with his last strength drove the axe straight into the fiend’s head. The blazing maw bellowed with pain and sank to the ground. Some sticky pitch gushed from the monster’s body. The beast staggered and roared with pain. Kondál does not tarry; he leaps into the air and strikes the second head. Then the third as well. The headless body of the beast thrashes in its death throes, and the young man, already half-fainting, hacks at the thorns that surround his beloved Svatava.

So the valiant Kondál saved himself, his sweetheart and the whole country around the hill of Žiar. The monster’s heads – as he had promised – he carried in a sack to the hut of the old Žrec below Javorník. Ever since, there has been peace in the bowels of Žiar.

Though some do claim that another inhabitant of some sort has moved into the underground chambers here. People no longer make so much noise, Žiar has grown over with forest again, and peace has spread into its secret nooks. And from the depths of the dragon’s hole in Mrská there is said to come, now and then, the dull rasping of a monster.
